summary.en: María Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela after months in exile, prompting protests demanding elections and her return. The United States has revived a torture indictment against Maduro for ordering torture of rivals and deployed Space Force electromagnetic and electronic warfare systems against Venezuela while pressuring Reliance to refine Venezuelan oil. CIA Director Ratcliffe visited Havana accompanied by a paramilitary operative linked to the operation that killed 32 Cuban soldiers, indicating a shift of U.S. covert focus toward Cuba. The Pentagon has prohibited DoD personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military actions involving Venezuela. UCDP counted 2 battle-related deaths in 2007.
summary.nb: María Corina Machado har returnert til Venezuela etter måneder i eksil, noe som har utløst protester som krever valg og hennes tilbakekomst. USA har gjenopptatt en torturanklage mot Maduro for å ha beordret tortur av rivaler og har satt i drift elektromagnetiske og elektroniske krigssystemer fra Space Force mot Venezuela, samtidig som de presser Reliance til å raffinere venezuelansk olje. CIA-direktør Ratcliffe besøkte Havana sammen med en paramilitær operativ knyttet til operasjonen som drepte 32 kubanske soldater, noe som indikerer et skifte i USAs hemmelige fokus mot Cuba. Pentagon har forbudt DoD-personell å bruke ikke-offentlig informasjon til å satse på amerikanske militære handlinger som involverer Venezuela. UCDP registrerte 2 kamprelaterte dødsfall i 2007.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
